items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He just lived around the corner from me.

ctx.x: About some of the other musicians in the area that you grew up in, was Russell Procope in that general vicinity?

Russell Procope was in that vicinity, indeed. He just lived around the corner from me. Oh, at that particular time, I guess he was studying the violin and the saxophone, but I don’t remember having heard him play at that time. But I know that he was a student of music.

items.title: 68146_Russell Procope oral history interview
items.q: And after I got through with this job there, then I -- then I joined Benny Carter. Of course Benny Carter was working at the Arcadia Ballroom.

ctx.x: Yeah, yeah. I worked there awhile and -- well, this was before Benny Carter. Yeah, I worked in a -- it wasn't a -- it was just a job. It wasn't too big. Nothing historical happened on this job. It was just a thing to help me on my way, as a matter of speaking.

And after I got through with this job there, then I -- then I joined Benny Carter. Of course Benny Carter was working at the Arcadia Ballroom. And that was a very, very -- very instructive, you know. That helped me greatly because Benny was making these great arrangements at that time, and then this was a time when before that most bands had three-part

saxophones. They played three part harmony. And it was just about that time that four part harmony came in, and as I remember it's a funny thing -- and that was the end of a whole lot of piano players, because they couldn't read the four part harmony on the piano, you know. So then a whole brand new -- it was a whole turnaround because musicians who were better schooled than the ones who were predominant before that, you know, then they came to power. But Benny was one of the first to write four part harmony for…
